title: Triphenyl phosphate may engage nuclear receptor-associated signaling and converge on an AHCY-centered lipid metabolic program in colorectal cancer: a hypothesis-driven network toxicology study with docking and multi-omics analysis
content:
Abstract
Triphenyl phosphate (TPhP) is a widely used organophosphate flame retardant and environmental contaminant. However, its potential mechanistic link to colorectal cancer (CRC) progression remains unclear. We applied a dual-evidence framework. Putative TPhP targets were intersected with CRC-associated genes for functional enrichment, protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, and hub prioritization. Molecular docking for prioritized nuclear receptor hubs was corroborated by CB-Dock2 and Protein–Ligand Interaction Profiler (PLIP). In parallel, a literature-guided AHCY–ACACA/SCD–METTL3 effector module was evaluated using transcriptomic data from TCGA and a CRC single-cell atlas. A total of 381 putative TPhP targets and 5,389 CRC-associated genes were compiled, yielding 176 shared candidates. Enrichment and hub analyses highlighted lipid metabolism-related processes and nuclear receptor-associated signaling. Docking showed plausible binding of TPhP to ESR1, PPARG, and AR, with predicted interactions dominated mainly by hydrophobic and π-related contacts. At the effector level, AHCY, SCD, ACACA, and METTL3 were upregulated in both TCGA-COAD and TCGA-READ tumors versus normal tissues. Single-cell atlas analysis further supported an AHCY-centered program, with the strongest malignant-cell enrichment observed for SCD, whereas ACACA and METTL3 provided supportive evidence. Furthermore, transcriptional co-expression analysis revealed a significant positive correlation between the upstream nuclear receptor signature and the downstream lipid metabolic effector module (r = 0.332, p = 2.79 × 10−11), delineating a regulatory bridge. This integrative analysis supports a plausible TPhP–nuclear receptor–linked lipid remodeling hypothesis and an AHCY-centered effector module in CRC. These findings outline a computational framework for future experimental hypothesis testing.
